title: Error Handling Strategies
description: Master error states, retry strategies, and error boundaries in React Query.

data.text: Every query and mutation in React Query has a rich set of error-related states. Understanding `isError`, `error`, and the retry system is essential for building applications that gracefully handle failures. React Query does not swallow errors silently â€” it surfaces them so you can decide exactly how your user should be informed.

terms.definition: A boolean flag on a query or mutation object that is true when the latest request resulted in an error.
The Error object returned by a failed query or mutation, containing a message and optional stack trace.
A configuration option (boolean or number) controlling how many times React Query will automatically retry a failed request.
A function or number that controls the wait time between automatic retries, typically used for exponential backoff.
A React component that catches JavaScript errors in its child tree and displays a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app.

data.text: When a query fails, React Query transitions through several states in order: the request starts, the error occurs, `isError` flips to `true`, the `error` property is populated, and then the retry logic activates if configured. If all retries are exhausted, `isError` remains `true` and it is your responsibility to display a user-facing error message.

data.caption: Flow diagram showing how React Query processes a failed request and applies retry logic before surfacing the error.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Request starts] --> B{HTTP response OK?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Cache data as success]
    B -->|No| D{Retries remaining?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Wait retryDelay ms]
    E --> A
    D -->|No| F[Set isError = true]
    F --> G[Populate error object]
    G --> H[Trigger onError callback]
    H --> I[User sees error UI]

data.text: React Query retries failed requests automatically, but the strategy matters. The simplest approach is `retry: false` â€” fail immediately. `retry: 3` retries three times with equal delay. For production APIs, exponential backoff is usually best, where delays grow between attempts to avoid overwhelming a struggling server.

rows: Avoids wasting requests on known failures

data.text: The simplest error display pattern checks `isError` and shows a message directly in the component. For larger apps, a global `onError` handler in the `QueryClient` can log or transform errors in one place, while individual components still decide what to show to the user.

data.title: Component-Level Error Handling
data.content: Displaying user-friendly error messages in a component using React Query v5.

data.text: React Query lets you set a global `onError` handler when you create your `QueryClient`. This is the right place for error logging, sending errors to a monitoring service like Sentry, or transforming error objects. It runs for every failed query across the entire application, so keep the logic minimal and focused.

data.title: Global Error Handler with React Query v5
data.content: Setting up a global error handler that logs errors and normalises the error object.

data.title: Log All Errors
data.text: A global onError handler ensures no error slips through silently. Hook it up to your error monitoring service from day one â€” it costs nothing and saves debugging time later.

Error boundaries catch render-time errors in React components. While React Query's `isError` state handles most data-fetching errors gracefully, errors thrown inside a render function (for example, accessing a property on `null` data before the guard runs) still crash the component tree. An error boundary catches these and shows a fallback UI.

data.title: Error Boundary Component
data.content: A React error boundary that catches unhandled render errors in React Query components.

data.title: Keep Boundaries Narrow
data.text: Wrap only the sections of your app that can actually throw â€” usually individual data-fetching components, not the whole application.

Raw error messages from the server are often confusing or expose internal details. The best practice is to map HTTP status codes to friendly messages in a central helper function, keeping the message consistent across your app and hiding implementation details from users.

data.title: Friendly Error Message Mapper
data.content: A utility function that converts API error responses into user-friendly messages.

items.question: What is the difference between isError and isFetchError?
items.answer: isError is true whenever the latest request fails. isFetchError is a more specific flag that is true only when the error came from a fetch operation (as opposed to a parse error, where isParseError is true).

items.question: Should I always use a global onError handler?
items.answer: It is strongly recommended. Use it for logging and monitoring. Component-level error handling should still be used to show user-facing messages â€” the global handler does not replace that.

items.question: What happens if all retries are exhausted?
items.answer: React Query sets isError to true and populates the error object with the last error received. Your component is then responsible for rendering an appropriate error state and optionally offering a retry button.

data.title: Exercise: Build a Robust Error Handling Layer
data.description: Practice implementing global error handling, retry policies, and error boundaries for a React Query application.
steps: Create a QueryClient with a global onError handler that logs errors to the console with the query key and error message.
Set retry to false for all mutations so failed POST requests surface immediately.
Configure retry: 3 with exponential backoff for GET queries but exclude 404 responses.
Build a QueryErrorBoundary class component that catches render-time errors and shows a fallback with a reload button.
Create a getFriendlyErrorMessage utility that maps HTTP status codes to human-readable strings.
Wire it all up in App.tsx and intentionally cause a 404 to verify the flow.
data.expectedOutcome: When a query fails, the global logger fires, retries run the configured number of times, and if all retries fail the error boundary catches any render crash while the user sees a friendly message with a retry button.

cards.title: No Retries
cards.description: The fastest way to fail. Best for mutations and POST requests.

cards.title: Fixed Retry Count
cards.description: Retry a set number of times with equal delays.

cards.title: Exponential Backoff
cards.description: Delays grow with each attempt, giving the server time to recover.

cards.title: Conditional Retry
cards.description: Retry only for specific error types, such as network errors or 5xx responses.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: isError and error surface every failed request in React Query
Use a global onError handler to centralise logging and monitoring
Configure retry and retryDelay per query type â€” use exponential backoff for flaky APIs
Error boundaries catch render-time crashes that isError cannot prevent
Map HTTP status codes to friendly messages for better user experience
data.takeaway: Good error handling is invisible to users â€” they see a helpful message and a retry button, not a crashed app.
